You have two options. Read the comparison, pick one, and follow only that section.

| | Posit Cloud | Local install |
|---|---|---|
| Time to start | About 1 minute | 20–40 minutes |
| Needs admin rights on the laptop | No | Yes |
| Works on a Chromebook or tablet | Yes | No |
| Works without internet | No | Yes |
| Free | Yes, with monthly hour limits | Yes, unlimited |
| Recommended for | Getting started quickly, lab sessions | Working offline, heavy use |

If you are unsure, start with Posit Cloud. You can switch to a local install later
without losing any work, because the notebooks are identical in both.

---

## Option A — Posit Cloud (no installation)

Posit Cloud runs R inside your web browser. Nothing is installed on your computer.

**Step 1.** Go to <https://posit.cloud> and click **Sign Up**. The free plan is
enough for this course.

**Step 2.** Your instructor will share a link to the course workspace. Click it,
then click **Save a Permanent Copy**. This gives you your own copy of all the
notebooks and data that you can edit freely.

**Step 3.** In the **Files** pane at the bottom right, open `1-Intro-to-R-Language` and click
`setup.R`. Then click the **Source** button at the top of the editor. Wait for it
to finish — the first run takes a few minutes because it downloads packages.

**Step 4.** When you see `SETUP COMPLETE`, you are ready. Open
`Fast-Intro-to-R.Rmd` and begin.

::: {.callout-warning title="Free-plan hours"}
The free plan gives you a limited number of compute hours per month. To avoid wasting
them, click the small **stop sign** icon on your project when you finish a session
rather than just closing the browser tab.
:::

## Option B — Local install (R + RStudio)

You must install **two** separate programs, in this order. R is the engine;
RStudio is the dashboard you actually work in. RStudio will not run without R.

### Step 1 — Install R

**Windows**

1. Go to <https://cran.r-project.org/bin/windows/base/>
2. Click **Download R for Windows** at the top.
3. Run the downloaded `.exe` file.
4. Accept every default. Do not change the install location.

**macOS**

1. Go to <https://cran.r-project.org/bin/macosx/>
2. Download the `.pkg` file. There are usually two — pick the one matching your
   chip. If your Mac was bought in 2021 or later it is almost certainly
   **Apple silicon (arm64)**. If you are not sure, click the Apple menu, then
   **About This Mac**, and look at the **Chip** or **Processor** line. "M1", "M2",
   "M3" or "M4" means arm64; "Intel" means the Intel version.
3. Run the `.pkg` and accept the defaults.

### Step 2 — Install RStudio

1. Go to <https://posit.co/download/rstudio-desktop/>
2. The page detects your operating system and offers the correct download. Scroll
   to step 2 on that page and click the download button.
3. Install it.
   - On **Windows**, run the `.exe` and accept the defaults.
   - On **macOS**, open the `.dmg` and drag the RStudio icon into your
     Applications folder.

### Step 3 — Check it worked

Open **RStudio** (not R — you should never need to open R directly again).

You will see several panes. The one on the left labelled **Console** is where R
prints things. Click into it, type the line below, and press Enter:

```r
2 + 2
```

If R replies with `[1] 4`, everything is working. The `[1]` is not part of the
answer — it is R telling you that this line of output starts at the first result.
You will see it constantly and can safely ignore it.

If you get an error instead, see Troubleshooting below.

### Step 4 — Get the course files

Copy the entire `R-Version` folder to somewhere sensible on your computer — your
Documents folder is fine. Do **not** leave it in Downloads, because you will
eventually clear that folder out and lose your work.

Then, in RStudio, use the menu: **File → Open File**, navigate to
`R-Version/1-Intro-to-R-Language/setup.R`, and open it.

### Step 5 — Run the setup script

With `setup.R` open, click the **Source** button in the top right of the editor
pane. The first run downloads several packages and may take five minutes. You will
see a lot of red text scroll past — this is normal. Red text in R is not
necessarily an error; it is just how R prints certain messages.

When you see `SETUP COMPLETE`, you are ready.

---

## Troubleshooting

**"RStudio cannot find an R installation."**
You installed RStudio but not R, or you installed them in the wrong order. Install
R (Step 1), then restart RStudio.

**A package fails to install with a message about compilation.**
R tried to build the package from source code instead of downloading a ready-made
version. Run this line in the Console and answer `no` if it asks whether to install
from source:

```r
install.packages("tidyverse", type = "binary")
```

**"Cannot open file ... No such file or directory" when reading the data.**
R is looking in the wrong folder. In RStudio use **Session → Set Working Directory
→ To Source File Location**, then run the chunk again. Part 0 explains why this
happens.

**Everything is tiny / the fonts are unreadable.**
**Tools → Global Options → Appearance** lets you change the editor font size and
theme.

**Nothing happens when I press Enter in the Console, and the prompt shows `+`.**
R thinks your command is unfinished — usually a missing closing bracket or quote.
Press **Esc** to cancel and start the line again.

---

## A note before you begin

Everyone finds their first week of R frustrating. Typos produce error messages that
look alarming and say nothing useful. This is normal and it passes quickly.

Two habits will save you most of that frustration:

1. **Read the error message.** It is usually more helpful than it first appears.
   `object 'sales' not found` genuinely means you have not created `sales` yet.
2. **Check your brackets and quotes.** The overwhelming majority of beginner errors
   are one missing `)` or `"`.

Do not worry if the code feels like memorisation at first. It stops feeling that
way around week three.
